newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada aims to minimize fallout from salmon spat.
newsitem.headline: Canada aims to minimize fallout from salmon spat.

text.p: Canadian politicians sought to defuse escalating tensions with the United States over Pacific salmon on Tuesday, after angry Canadian fishermen lifted their blockade of an Alaskan ferry.

"It is essential to keep the focus on the fishery...we have to maintain the moral high ground," a spokeswoman for Canadian Fisheries Minister David Anderson said in a telephone interview from Prince Rupert, British Columbia.
"But when we let this issue get unfocused and refocused on other issues...we begin to lose that moral high ground," the spokeswoman said.

She spoke after Canadian fishermen late on Monday lifted a three-day blockade of an Alaskan ferry following a court order. During the blockade, some fishermen angered ferry passengers by burning an American flag. The ferry was on its way to Alaska on Tuesday.

Alaska Senator Frank Murkowski hinted at retaliation for the incident on Monday. Canada's Anderson has acknowledged that the Americans could harm Canadian ferry routes by prohibiting access through U.S. waters close to Vancouver.
Canadians fear bitterness from the salmon dispute could spread over into trade issues where Canada is vulnerable.

"They can always hurt us more than we can hurt them," said political scientist Edelgard Mahant at York University in Toronto. "So we have to make an effort to negotiate at the senior level in Washington."
The ferry blockade came amid a long-running dispute over salmon quotas.

Late last week, the Canadian government sent the United States a diplomatic note accusing it of violating an international treaty late last week. British Columbia Premier Glen Clark wrote an open letter to U.S. President Bill Clinton urging him to halt the commercial fishing of Pacific salmon.
The outspoken premier has also threatened to close down a torpedo testing range used by the U.S. military at Nanoose Bay, near Vancouver.
Canadian cabinet ministers have urged Clark to withdraw his threat to close the testing range.
"We are now back to where we can negotiate with the Americans once again," Anderson told CBC Newsworld on Tuesday.
"It was impossible when the ferry was held at the dock... I also think if we remove Nanoose Bay from the table, we'll have much more chance with the Americans in negotiations."

After months of stormy talks with Washington about how to divide this year's Pacific salmon catch, Canada accused the United States last week of overfishing Canada-bound sockeye salmon and violating an international treaty.
But the United States has replied that the bountiful sockeye salmon catch this year was "incidental" to an abundant catch of pink salmon.
U.S. officials have denied breaching any international agreements and said Canada was responsible for the breakdown in talks last spring.
Canadians fear the heated rhetoric will turn into a tit-for-tat scrap that will hurt Canadian trade interests.

"We can just imagine how some U.S. senators are relishing the chance to use the Pacific salmon dispute to settle a few trade scores close to their own hearts -- whether it's Canadian grain sales or softwood lumber or the Canada-U.S. auto pact or potatoes or the huge overall trade imbalance," an editorial in the tabloid Ottawa Sun said on Tuesday."
